turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab a pressure and a pulse before you go in, just sit easy there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I will of course, I've been sitting out there an age, the radio was going and some fella talking about the hurling, I wasn't even following it, my mind was on the legs.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Grand so. Blood pressure is one forty two over eighty six, pulse is seventy eight, and your oxygen is ninety seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the oxygen the important bit? Years ago in the hospital with the flu they said a different number but that was a whole other story, I was in a ward with six of us.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. That's only today's. Doctor's ready for you now.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): In you come. How are you keeping these days?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure I'm not bad in myself at all, doctor, it's the legs that have me in.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on so, tell me about the legs.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's cramps in the two calves, at night. I'm two months at it, nearly every night, and they wake me out of the sleep.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It begins with a little twitch, err, and then the calf just locks, like someone has a fist in there, and I'm out on the landing walking up and down, and then I put the kettle on even though I won't drink the tea.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): What eases it when that happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The walking eases it, and if I rub the calf hard with my hand. The hot water bottle was useless, I gave up on that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you get any swelling in the ankles or the legs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling at all. I check them in the morning and they're ordinary, no puff in them.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or are you getting breathless walking on the flat?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort. Down to the shop and back I'm grand, the breathing doesn't bother me, it's purely the nights.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the waterworks and the bowels, any change?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No change, they're as they always were. I go regular enough and there's no burning or anything like that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And what tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Well there's a few. Amlodipine five milligrams with the breakfast, that's for the pressure. I've a long history with that tablet but you don't need the whole saga.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the water tablet, forty milligrams, every morning, the little white one. On the box the chemist has frusemide, but everyone at home calls it the water tablet.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): At night I take the cholesterol one, atorvastin twenty milligrams, for the cholesterol. And my sugar tablets are metformin, five hundred milligrams in the morning and again with the tea, for the sugar.

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and only the magnesium from the shop as well. I got it in the chemist on Patrick Street, two hundred milligrams, one at bedtime, for these cramps. I'm about three weeks taking that.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you getting all of those in, the way they're supposed to be taken?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The prescription ones, yes, they're in a box by the kettle and I don't miss them. The magnesium, umm, I forget it. Maybe four nights in the week I actually take it, I couldn't swear to which nights.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about fluids, how much are you drinking?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Very little water, doctor, I'll admit it. Two small cups of tea in the day and that's the height of it. With the water tablet I'm afraid of being up half the night, and the bathroom window doesn't even close properly, there's a draught.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I follow you. May I have a look at the legs?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): You may of course. Don't mind the hole in the left sock, I've been saying I'll mend it since Christmas and I haven't.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Calves are soft, no tenderness there. Pulses are present in both feet. The ankles are a bit puffy, both sides.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Are they now. Well actually, by the evening they do puff up. The shoes get tight and the elastic of the socks leaves a mark, the two ankles, and that's been a few weeks. They're grand again in the morning so I put it out of my head.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So they swell by evening and settle overnight.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it exactly. Just the ankles, not up the leg.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working thought is these night cramps are linked with the water tablet and how little you're drinking, because the potassium can drop on frusemide. I don't want to call it for certain until the bloods are back.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'm booking blood tests, the kidney function and the potassium, and the magnesium too while you're on the shop one.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put you down for Thursday morning in the clinic. No fasting for those.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday is fine, I have bowls but I'll skip the start. The half eight bus is reliable, Mrs Kearney from two doors down gets it as well, she talks the whole way.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, stretch the calves before bed. Both of them, hold it about half a minute, and do a few on each side.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Half a minute, a few each side, I can do that in the kitchen. Should I stay on the magnesium?

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay on the same two hundred at bedtime for now. Try and sip a bit more water through the day, nice and steady, not buckets of it. And don't start any other bits from the shop.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't, no. There was an ayurvedic powder sitting on the shelf and I looked at it twice, but I never bought it and I certainly never took any.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in two weeks, whether the results are in or not.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, I'll write it on the calendar beside the bins day. Am I to keep the water tablet going the same?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep it the same, forty milligrams in the morning. Don't stop it yourself.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): And say the cramp is desperate on a given night, would you give me something for the pain of it?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't add a painkiller today. Let's see what the tests say before we add anything.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Your blood form will be at the desk, so Thursday is booked.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely, thanks very much. I'll start the stretches tonight so.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Medication, dose, timing, indication supported; generic name is stated as 'atorvastin,' not atorvastatin.
bad.text: cholesterol tablet (generic_name=atorvastatin, dose=20 mg, frequency=at night, indication=the cholesterol, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Calf cramps wake the patient from sleep and start with a little twitch before the calf 'locks'.

Patient initially denied any swelling ('No swelling at all'), but later clarified that both ankles do swell by evening for a few weeks, shoes get tight and sock elastic leaves marks, and the swelling is limited to the ankles and settles by morning.
Negative finding asked and answered: no leg or calf tenderness was reported by the patient before exam.
Blood tests were specifically booked for Thursday morning in clinic, with no fasting required.
Doctor advised not to add a painkiller today and to wait for blood test results before adding anything.
